strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored problem: scalable joint generation of hypergraph topology and node features, with an extension to graphs, and demonstrates the ability to handle larger point-cloud graphs where flat baselines (DiGress/DeFoG) run out of memory.

Builds on strong hierarchical coarsening/expansion frameworks and adds a budget mechanism and minibatch OT coupling; provides algorithms, proofs, complexity analysis, and hyperparameter settings, which improves reproducibility over many graph-generation papers.

Experiments cover synthetic hypergraphs, 3D meshes, and graph point clouds; FAHNES achieves substantial improvements in several key metrics over HYGENE (e.g., SBM Valid 87.8 vs 65.0; Ego NumDiff 0.128 vs 12.550; Tree Valid 89.7 vs 77.5) and over the sequential mesh baseline (Manifold40 airplane ChamDist 0.048 vs 0.143).
Ablation studies show that the budget mechanism and OT coupling can help, especially on feature-based metrics such as ChamDist on ManifoldNet.
Limitations are acknowledged, including scalability pressure and simple feature assumptions, and the paper is generally well-structured and clear.
weaknesses: Feature generation is only validated for 3D node coordinates (mesh vertices/point coordinates) with no edge or hyperedge feature generation in the experiments, despite the abstract and introduction framing the contribution as generating node and edge/hyperedge features jointly. This greatly narrows the empirical support for the central “feature-aware” claim.

No rich, categorical, or heterogeneous feature distributions are tested; the only feature-aware baseline is a sequential disjoint baseline trained on ground-truth topology, and there is no comparison to feature-aware hypergraph/graph generative models on small or medium featured hypergraphs.

Feature-quality metrics are weak: ChamDist to the nearest training sample does not measure distributional fidelity or coverage, and novelty/uniqueness metrics for meshes/point clouds are not reported, leaving open the possibility of memorization or nearest-neighbor artifacts.

Ablation results are mixed and not statistically robust; budgets and OT coupling sometimes hurt or yield overlapping confidence intervals (e.g., Tree hypergraphs Valid 89.7±4.0 with budgets vs 90.7±4.7 without; Ego NumDiff 0.128 with both vs 0.073 without OT; ManifoldNet Bench Spectral/Harmonic/Closeness better without OT). The claims that these components clearly improve quality/stability are overstated.

Theoretical contributions are limited: Proposition 3 proves standard MSE minimization but assumes an unweighted arithmetic mean while the method uses budget-weighted averaging; the OT-coupling results are informal or essentially restate that picking the minimum cost within a restricted set shortens paths, without full analysis of the flow-matching objective.

Novelty is incremental relative to [9], [10], [12], [13], [23]; the core coarsen-expand pipeline, spectral coarsening, Local PPGN architecture, and OT coupling are adapted from prior work, while the main new budget mechanism is an architectural extension.

The scalability claim is partially contradicted by the limitations section: the method still struggles on very large hypergraphs (ModelNet Bookshelf/Piano) and large point clouds, and no runtime/memory comparisons are provided; flat baselines going OOM alone does not establish efficient scaling.

Baseline selection is weak for featured hypergraphs and 3D meshes: the sequential baseline is not a published state-of-the-art method, and HYGENE is featureless. The paper’s “state-of-the-art” framing is therefore not fully justified by the experimental design.

Some reported baseline numbers and comparisons are unusual (e.g., HYGENE Node Num 42.520 on ModelNet Piano vs FAHNES 0.846; large synthetic metric differences) and would benefit from additional validation, statistical tests, and discussion of possible hyperparameter mismatch.

strengths: Addresses a relevant and challenging problem: joint generation of topology and features for hypergraphs at scale.
Proposes a hierarchical coarsening-expansion framework that logically extends prior topology-only methods (e.g., HYGENE) to include feature generation.
The node budget mechanism is an intuitive and potentially useful idea for controlling local growth and maintaining consistency across scales.
Demonstrates scalability on point cloud datasets where flat baselines (DiGress, DeFoG) run out of memory, highlighting a practical advantage.
The empirical results on synthetic hypergraph datasets (SBM, Ego, Tree) show high validity scores and improvements over HYGENE.
The paper includes extensive appendices with proofs, implementation details, and additional results, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: The theoretical justification for the node budget mechanism is weak. Proposition 3 trivially proves that averaging features minimizes MSE, which is a basic statistical fact and does not provide any insight into why the budget mechanism specifically improves hierarchical consistency or generative performance.

The claimed advantage of budgets over previous 'cluster size vectors' [9, 10] is not convincingly established. The ablation studies (Tables 4 and 5) show only marginal, inconsistent improvements when budgets are used (e.g., on Tree, removing budgets sometimes improves Validity). The paper does not rigorously analyze why budgets lead to better global coherence.

Minibatch OT-coupling, presented as a key contribution, is overly complex and its practical benefit is unclear. The constrained formulation (Eq. 9) and the restrictive equivalence assumption (only within a cluster) reduce its impact. The theoretical proofs (Propositions 10 and 12) are based on strong and questionable assumptions (e.g., node equivalence), and the ablation results (Tables 4 and 5) do not consistently demonstrate significant improvements.
The empirical evaluation is insufficient to support the claim of state-of-the-art feature-aware generation.

- For 3D meshes, the only baseline is a sequential version of their own method. Comparing against a self-designed weaker variant is not a convincing evaluation of the joint generation capability. No comparisons to other specialized mesh generation models (e.g., PolyGen, MeshGPT) are made.

- On some datasets (e.g., ModelNet Piano, Bench Point Clouds), the error bars (twice standard deviation) are very large, indicating high variance and calling into question the statistical significance of the reported mean results.

- Core claims about scalability and performance are supported by selective comparisons. The OOM results for DiGress and DeFoG are mentioned but do not provide a quality comparison for the point cloud datasets.

The novelty of the work is incremental. The core pipeline (coarsen-expand + flow-matching) is adapted directly from prior work (HYGENE, [9]). The main innovations, node budgets and OT-coupling, are either not new conceptually (budgets are similar to existing cluster size vectors) or offer unclear practical advantage.

The scope of 'feature-aware generation' is narrow. Evaluation is limited to 3D coordinates (node positions). The method is not tested on datasets with categorical, discrete, or heterogeneous features (e.g., atom types in molecules), which is a significant limitation given the motivation.

Presentation quality is mixed. Figures 4 and 11 show generated 3D meshes that are qualitatively poor (e.g., pianos look like blobs, airplanes are fragmented), which undermines the claim of high-quality feature generation. The ablation tables (e.g., Table 4) are confusingly laid out with misaligned headers and notation.

The limitations section is honest but, given the overreaching claims in the abstract and introduction, it reads as a list of fundamental weaknesses (e.g., struggles with large structures, assumes simple feature distributions) rather than minor caveats.

The paper lacks a clear explanation for how the point cloud dataset (1024 nodes) was split into 128 training/32 validation/40 testing. Such a massive dataset would typically have a different split, raising questions about data leakage or a misstatement.

strengths: Introduces a well-motivated framework (FAHNES) for jointly generating hypergraph topology and features at scale, addressing a genuine gap since prior hierarchical methods ([9],[10]) handle only unfeatured structures.

The node budget mechanism is a principled and useful refinement over the cluster-size-vector conditioning of prior work, with a simple supporting result (Prop. 3 on mean-minimizing MSE) and empirical support in the ablations.

Extends minibatch OT-coupling to the hierarchical (hyper)graph setting with permutation constraints restricted to equivalent nodes, which is a sensible adaptation with a marginal-preservation argument (Prop. 10).

Strong and consistent quantitative gains over HYGENE across SBM, Ego, Tree, and ModelNet40 hypergraph datasets, and clear improvement over the sequential disjoint baseline on the featured 3D mesh tasks.

Reproducibility is well supported: detailed coarsening/expansion/refinement definitions, full training and sampling algorithms, hyperparameters, architecture description, and a complexity analysis are provided in the appendices.
The limitations section is candid about residual scaling difficulties, feature-distribution assumptions, and training cost.
weaknesses: The featured-hypergraph evaluation (the paper's central claim) compares only against a self-constructed sequential baseline; no comparison to other featured generative models is provided, which weakens the 'state-of-the-art in jointly generating features and structure' claim.

The graph point cloud comparison is effectively vacuous: DiGress and DeFoG are OOM, so Table 3 demonstrates feasibility only, not superiority. The paper's scalability claim would be stronger with a working baseline at a reduced scale.

There is a numerical inconsistency: Section 4.2 reports Chamfer distances of 0.073 (bench) and 0.049 (airplane), while Appendix Table 7 reports 0.064 (bench) and 0.048 (airplane). These numbers should be reconciled.

The OT-coupling ablation is ambiguous and partly undermines the claimed contribution: it helps on some datasets but not others, and on Tree removing both components yields a higher Valid score (95.6 vs 89.7), suggesting the benefit is not robust across settings.
The 'Ratio' metric in Table 3 takes very large values (e.g., 67.3±44.9, 84.4±0.000) that are not clearly explained or interpreted, making it hard to assess generative quality from that column.
Theoretical results (Props. 3, 8, 10, 12) are fairly standard (mean minimizes MSE; OT coupling preserves marginals and shortens paths) and provide limited new insight.

Novelty is incremental: the framework is a substantial extension of [9]/[10], and the core coarsen-expand pipeline is inherited; the main new elements are feature integration, the budget mechanism, and OT-coupling.
Baseline comparisons in Table 1 report single values for HYGENE versus mean±std for FAHNES, which makes the fairness of the comparison unclear.

strengths: The paper introduces FAHNES, a hierarchical generative framework that jointly models topology and features for both graphs and hypergraphs, extending prior hierarchical approaches (Bergmeister et al., 2024; Gailhard et al., 2025) that only generate topology. This is a meaningful and practically relevant contribution, since features (e.g., 3D coordinates in meshes) are essential in many applications.

The hierarchical scale encoding is a genuine conceptual improvement over the cluster-size vectors of prior work: by tracking the total number of absorbed nodes per cluster and recursively redistributing it during expansion, the model gains local control over growth and improves global consistency. The ablation (Table 5) generally supports its benefit, especially for feature-based metrics (ChamDist).

The multi-scale graph OT coupling is a principled adaptation of minibatch OT to hierarchical graph generation, and Propositions 2 and 3 provide reasonable (if standard) guarantees on marginal preservation and displacement variance reduction. The overhead is claimed to be small (~4%), which is plausible given the restriction to intra-cluster permutations of size 2-3.

The complexity analysis (Appendix H) and the point-cloud experiment (Table 3), where all flat baselines (Flow Matching, DiGress, DeFoG) run OOM, credibly demonstrate quasi-linear scaling to large featured structures. This is the key practical argument for the method.

Reproducibility is good: the code is open-sourced, hyperparameters (layers, dimensions, sampling steps, optimizer) are given for all experiment families, and the algorithms (training, sampling, coarsening, OT coupling) are provided in the appendix.
The limitations section is honest about remaining scalability issues (very large hypergraphs such as ModelNet bookshelf/piano), the restriction to continuous features, and training cost.
weaknesses: Several central claims are somewhat overstated. On SBM graphs (Table 2), FAHNES achieves 50.0% valid vs. DeFoG's 90.0% and DiGress's 60.0%, i.e., it is clearly worse than flat methods on this dataset, which weakens the 'competitive or state-of-the-art' framing for graphs. The abstract's claim of 'competitive or state-of-the-art performance' is only partially supported.

Comparison with featureless baselines is not entirely apples-to-apples: FAHNES reports mean±std over 5 runs, while baseline numbers are single values taken from prior work (Bergmeister et al., 2024; Qin et al., 2025). This makes the improvements difficult to interpret statistically, and no significance assessment is given.

The theoretical results are mostly standard and do not constitute strong novel theory: Proposition 1 (the barycenter minimizes MSE) is a textbook result; Propositions 2-3 are direct adaptations of minibatch-OT guarantees; Proposition 4 is informal ('asymptotic dominance of S') and not rigorously stated. The propositions mainly justify implementation choices rather than deepening understanding.

On point-cloud graphs (Table 9), the reported Ratio metrics are very high (67.3±44.9 for aircraft, 73.3±22.2 for bench), suggesting poor structural fidelity despite the low Chamfer distance. The paper does not explain or discuss this discrepancy, and these results are not presented in the main text.

For the featured mesh datasets (Table 4), the baselines are weak (sequential, WGAN, Flow Matching, VAE on padded incidence images). No strong featured graph/hypergraph generative model is compared, so the evidence that joint generation is necessary is weaker than claimed.

Ablation results are mixed and occasionally contradict the paper's narrative. In Table 5 for ManifoldNet Bench, removing both scale encoding and coupling gives a higher ChamCov (42.2) than the full model (42.2) and removing OT coupling also gives 42.2; the claim that 'lacking one of them results in much worse results' is not uniform across metrics, and some differences are within standard deviations.

Notation in Section 3.5 is confusing: B is used both for the bipartite graph and as minibatch size in Eq. 6 (X, Y ∈ R^{B×d}, Π_n), and Π_B is described as 'B×B permutations' inconsistent with Π_n in the objective. This makes the OT formulation harder to verify.

The mechanism for feature generation (FiLM conditioning on parent features, following Ren et al., 2025) is described only briefly; the main text does not clearly explain how continuous features are predicted and propagated, nor how the method handles feature-domain differences (Gaussian vs. Dirichlet priors) beyond a short implementation note.

strengths: Addresses a clear and useful gap: hierarchical generative modeling with node/hyperedge features for graphs and hypergraphs, including higher-order structures.
The hierarchical scale encoding gives local control over cluster growth and enables exact target node counts; ablations suggest it improves over simply concatenating a global target size.
The multi-scale OT coupling is lightweight in practice and can improve training stability/alignment on some datasets.
The empirical study spans synthetic, 3D mesh, and point-cloud data, and demonstrates scaling to featured structures where flat baselines report OOM.
The paper is generally well organized, and the limitations section honestly acknowledges remaining scalability and feature-domain constraints.
weaknesses: Novelty is incremental: the core coarsen-expand architecture closely follows Bergmeister et al. (2024) and Gailhard et al. (2025); feature averaging and scale encodings are natural extensions. The 'first' claim is weakened by existing hierarchical molecular models with features (e.g., MolGrow, MolHF), even if general-graph applicability differs.

The central claim of effective joint topology-feature generation is not convincingly evaluated. For 3D meshes, baselines are weak/naive (image-based VAE/GAN/flow matching, sequential disjoint generation) rather than strong feature-aware graph/mesh generators. DiGress/DeFoG are omitted for the 50-node mesh datasets despite being run on larger unfeatured graphs. Featured point-cloud experiments have no comparison method at all, so the 'state-of-the-art' framing is not established.

Several theoretical results are weak or overstated. Proposition 1 is a standard barycenter result; Proposition 3 compares OT coupling only to the identity permutation and follows trivially from minimizing over a set containing identity; Proposition 4 is informal, with no conditions or quantification. The probabilistic factorization in Eq. (10) is not justified under the stated assumptions.

There are implementation/algorithmic inconsistencies and missing details. Algorithm 2 handles only clusters of size 2, while the text and problem setup allow clusters producing 2 or 3 children. Scale-encoding splitting via ceil does not necessarily sum back to the parent scale encoding, but the rounding correction is not fully specified. The mesh reconstruction and surface sampling used to compute Chamfer metrics are not detailed, making the featured mesh results hard to interpret or reproduce.

Ablation results do not consistently support the claimed importance of the components. OT coupling sometimes worsens metrics (e.g., ModelNet Bookshelf spectral, ManifoldNet Airplane ChamCov), and the full model is occasionally beaten by an ablated variant on individual metrics, undermining claims that the proposed components are 'essential'.

Some evaluation choices make improvements less meaningful: node-count differences can be trivially reduced by conditioning on the target size, and 'competitive' claims on SBM graphs overlook that DeFoG/DiGress obtain substantially higher validity. Main-table summaries also omit numerous metrics on which FAHNES is worse than HYGENE or HSpectre.

Presentation issues remain: inconsistent reference years, no visible code URL despite the open-source claim, and several broad claims in the abstract/introduction that go beyond what the experiments support.

strengths: Addresses a clear and important gap: scalable joint generation of topology and features for graphs and hypergraphs, extending hierarchical graph generation beyond featureless structures.

Introduces useful technical components, especially the hierarchical scale encoding for local growth control and multi-scale OT coupling for aligning expanded duplicates; ablations show consistent improvements on several datasets.

Broad empirical evaluation across synthetic hypergraphs/graphs, 3D meshes, and point clouds, with strong results on featureless hypergraphs and graphs, and the only method that scales to large point clouds where DiGress/DeFoG run out of memory.
Provides theoretical analysis and detailed appendices, algorithms, and hyperparameters; open-source code supports reproducibility.
Honestly discusses limitations, including remaining failures on very large structures and restriction to continuous feature distributions.
weaknesses: Empirical validation of edge/hyperedge feature generation is missing: all featured experiments use only node features (3D coordinates), despite the abstract emphasizing node and edge features as critical.

Baseline comparisons for featured 3D meshes are limited to simple adapted models (VAE, WGAN, flow matching, sequential disjoint generation); modern graph/mesh generative baselines are not compared, and mesh-specific validity/manifoldness metrics are absent.

The multi-scale OT coupling is restricted to local permutations among 2–3 sibling nodes within a cluster and does not solve global graph permutation alignment; the theoretical contribution is therefore more modest than the framing suggests.

Minor theoretical inconsistency: Proposition 1 states the unweighted cluster barycenter as optimal, but the coarsening implementation uses scale-encoding-weighted averaging, and the proof does not cover the weighted case.

The quasi-linear complexity claim may not hold for hypergraphs with large hyperedges because coarsening operates on the clique expansion; experiments only use small hyperedges (≤5). Several reference-year errors and typos should also be corrected.
